title: Evidence for Chapter 27: the gold standard between the wars, 1919-1929
source: Hansard (Commons, 28 April 1925; Lords, 11 May 1925); the Gold Standard Act 1925; Keynes (1923, 1925); the Macmillan Committee's Minutes of Evidence (1930); Brown (1940); Nurkse (1944); Dulles (1929); De Long and Shleifer (1990); McGrattan and Prescott (2003); Federal Reserve History (2013); Rappoport and White (1991); Dutton (1984, with the comment by Moggridge); Sveriges Riksbank; Wikisource; the authority records of the Bibliothèque nationale de France
series: Evidence rows: id, place, year, values (';' separated, in the order of the quotation), unit, source key, page or column, the source text verbatim, note
license: Quotations for criticism, scholarship and teaching, each with its source; no full original is redistributed. Hansard (the Commons debates of 28 April 1925, the Lords debate of 11 May 1925 and the people pages): 'Contains Parliamentary information licensed under the Open Parliament Licence v3.0.' The Gold Standard Act 1925 (legislation.gov.uk): 'Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0.' The Macmillan Committee's Minutes of Evidence (HMSO, 1931) and Nurkse's International Currency Experience (League of Nations, 1944) are official publications; the Crown publication is older than fifty years and out of Crown copyright, and the League of Nations volume is quoted briefly with its source. Keynes (1883-1946): A Tract on Monetary Reform (1923) and The Economic Consequences of Mr. Churchill (1925) are in the public domain in the United Kingdom. Brown (1940), NBER: 'Copyright, 1940, by National Bureau of Economic Research, Inc. ... All Rights Reserved' (row br_copyright); short quotations only, with full credit. De Long and Shleifer (1990), NBER Working Paper 3523 (no copyright line is printed on the PDF), and McGrattan and Prescott (2003), Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis Staff Report 294: in copyright; short phrases only, the rest paraphrased. Dulles (1929, 'All rights reserved', published March 1929): short quotations. Federal Reserve History (2013) and the Riksbank's timeline: cited for facts in short quotations; for the Riksbank page: 'Enter source, Sveriges riksbank and date.' Wikisource (fr): CC BY-SA, cited for dates. The chapter's Chinese renders the quotations; the translations are the book's. The authority records of the Bibliothèque nationale de France (data.bnf.fr) are metadata reused under the Licence Ouverte (Open License). NBER working papers (De Long and Shleifer 1990; Rappoport and White 1991) are quoted in short phrases with their source.
notes: Every quotation is checked word for word against the cached source text by data/fetch/verify_web_quotes.py, and every value is read from its quotation by checks/check_ch27.py. Norman's answers to the Macmillan Committee (Q. 3353-63, in a volume not obtained) are indirect testimony, through Brown (1940); the report of the Committee on the Currency and Bank of England Note Issues (Chamberlain-Bradbury, 1925, Cmd. 2393) is known here only through the Earl of Clarendon's reading of its paragraph 15 in the Lords, and the Cunliffe Committee's report (1918) only through Churchill, Clarendon, Lord Hunsdon (who signed it) and Nurkse. Moreau's account of his talks with Norman (Revue des Deux Mondes) is cited by Brown and not quoted here. OCR misprints are kept in the quotations and named in the notes; Hansard's column numbers come from the page's column anchors.
